fact: There are fewer cache lines than main memory blocks, which is why a mapping function is needed to decide how main memory blocks go into cache lines
Three techniques can be used for mapping blocks into cache lines: direct, associative and set associative
Direct mapping is the simplest technique and maps each block of main memory into only one possible cache line
The direct mapping function is expressed as i equals j modulo m, where i is the cache line number, j is the main memory block number and m is the number of lines in the cache
To determine whether a block is in a direct mapped cache, use the line field of the memory address to index the cache line and compare the tag from the memory address with the line tag
If the tags match it is a cache hit, and the corresponding word is retrieved from the indexed cache line
If the tags do not match it is a cache miss, and the indexed cache line is updated with the word and the tag
The advantage of direct mapping is that it is simple and inexpensive to implement

The disadvantage of direct mapping is that there is a fixed cache location for any given block, so if a program references words repeatedly from two different blocks that map into the same line the blocks will be continually swapped in the cache and the hit ratio will be low, which is known as thrashing

Worked direct mapping example 1 considers a direct mapped cache of size 16 KB with block size 256 bytes and a main memory of 128 KB, and asks for the number of bits in the tag and the tag directory size
Block size, frame size and line size all mean the same thing in the worked cache examples
In the worked examples the memory is taken to be byte addressable, so a main memory of 128 KB is 2 to the power 17 bytes and the physical address is 17 bits
A block size of 256 bytes is 2 to the power 8 bytes, so the number of bits in the block offset is 8 bits

The total number of lines in cache is the cache size divided by the line size, so 16 KB over 256 bytes is 2 to the power 14 over 2 to the power 8, which is 2 to the power 6 lines, giving a line number of 6 bits
The number of bits in the tag is the number of bits in the physical address minus the sum of the line number bits and the block offset bits, so 17 minus 6 plus 8, which is 17 minus 14, giving 3 bits
Tag directory size is the number of tags times the tag size, which is the number of lines in cache times the number of bits in the tag, so 2 to the power 6 times 3 bits is 192 bits, that is 24 bytes
Associative mapping overcomes the disadvantage of direct mapping by permitting each main memory block to be loaded into any line of the cache
In associative mapping the cache control logic interprets a memory address simply as a Tag and a Word field, and the Tag field uniquely identifies a block of main memory
To determine whether a block is in a fully associative cache, the cache control logic must simultaneously examine every line's tag for a match
In associative mapping the Tag is s bits and uniquely identifies a block of main memory, while the Word field is w bits and uniquely identifies a word within a block
If a match exists in the associative comparison it is a cache hit, and the tag field of the memory address is used to index the cache line and retrieve the corresponding word
If no match exists it is a cache miss, and a cache line must be chosen and then updated with the word and the tag

Worked associative example 1 considers a fully associative mapped cache of size 16 KB with block size 256 bytes and a main memory of 128 KB, and asks for the number of bits in the tag and the tag directory size
In worked associative example 1 the main memory of 128 KB is 2 to the power 17 bytes, so the physical address is 17 bits, and the block size of 256 bytes is 2 to the power 8 bytes
In fully associative mapping the number of bits in the tag is the number of bits in the physical address minus the number of bits in the block offset, so 17 minus 8 gives 9 bits
In worked associative example 1 the total number of lines in cache is 16 KB over 256 bytes, that is 2 to the power 14 over 2 to the power 8, which is 2 to the power 6 lines
In worked associative example 1 the tag directory size is the number of lines times the number of bits in the tag, 2 to the power 6 times 9 bits, which is 576 bits, that is 72 bytes
Worked associative example 2 has a block size of 4 KB and a main memory of 16 GB, which is 2 to the power 34 bytes
In worked associative example 2 the physical address is 34 bits, the block size of 4 KB is 2 to the power 12 bytes giving a 12-bit block offset, so the tag is 34 minus 12, which is 22 bits
The solution slide for associative example 2 is repeated, restating that the physical address is 34 bits, the block offset is 12 bits and the tag is 22 bits
Set associative mapping is an enhanced form of direct mapping in which the drawbacks of direct mapping are removed, and it addresses the problem of possible thrashing in the direct mapping method

Instead of having exactly one line that a block can map to, set associative mapping groups a few lines together to create a set, and a block in memory can map to any one of the lines of a specific set

Set-associative mapping allows each word present in the cache to have two or more words in main memory for the same index address, and it combines the best of the direct and associative cache mapping techniques
Worked set associative example 1 considers a 2-way set associative mapped cache of size 16 KB with block size 256 bytes and a main memory of 128 KB, so the set size is 2

In worked set associative example 1 the main memory of 128 KB is 2 to the power 17 bytes giving a 17-bit physical address, and the block size of 256 bytes is 2 to the power 8 bytes giving an 8-bit block offset
In worked set associative example 1 the total number of lines in cache is 16 KB over 256 bytes, which is 64 lines
The total number of sets in cache is the total number of lines divided by the set size, so 64 over 2 is 32 sets, which is 2 to the power 5, so the set number is 5 bits
